Caring Village
Direct (coordination)
Family care-coordination apps
https://caringvillage.com/
One shared app for a family's care: calendar, to-dos, medication lists, care plan, journal, group messages, document storage, and an AI helper called Julia.
Claims to be one 'command center' that replaces scattered texts and spreadsheets, built by former caregivers, with a 24/7 AI assistant.

Keeps the whole family updated and on the same page (10 of 29), puts the loved one's care in one place (8), and is easy to use (7). Families mainly use the shared calendar (6) and medication lists (6), and say it means less stress (5) and less back-and-forth than texting (3).

Small, scattered complaints, none bigger than 3: the daily care plan resets or is too rigid (3), bugs and lost entries (3), 'friends' can see private medical details (2), medication logs don't show who gave a dose (2), and it's hard to get everyone into the group (2).

Mostly positive: praise themes reach 10, and no complaint theme is bigger than 3. Writers are mostly adult siblings sharing a parent's care. Caution: 13 of the 5-star reviews came from Sept 2025 to Apr 2026 with similar wording. Most detailed complaints are from 2019 and 2020. Caregivers on Reddit almost never name it (3 posts, none describing use).

It organizes information but can't make relatives help, the biggest caregiver problem (217 posts), and families say getting everyone to join is hard. It doesn't help with getting into the parent's bank, insurer or portal accounts (132 posts), doesn't help with POA problems (97), and has no safety or alert side (59). Few caregivers know it exists.
One free app where the whole family coordinates a loved one's care together, so no one carries it alone.
Freemium subscription. A free plan with ads, plus paid Circle and Village plans. It also sells to businesses for their patients or clients, and offers gift subscriptions. No funding figure found.

The caregiver who creates the 'village' pays. Everyone invited joins free. Free: 2 members. Circle: $14.99 a month (5 members). Village: $24.99 a month (50 members on the pricing page, 25 in the FAQ). 17% off yearly.

The free plan's 2-member limit pushes larger families to pay, and daily to-dos, reminders and journal likes bring people back. Reviewers who stay use it daily for a long time (5). Use ends when the loved one dies (2).
Self-serve: a help center, a support email, guided setup, checklists and the Julia AI assistant. No phone support or hours are listed. Reviewers say the support team answers quickly (3).

Yes. The creator invites relatives, friends and paid helpers, and each joins free with their own account and a role. Reviewers confirm big families share one group (5), but report limits on who can join and what they see (4).

Encrypted and never sold. Only members see the data, by roles the creator sets. Deletion is by emailing support. How to remove one member isn't stated. Reviewers worry that 'friends' can see private medical details (2).
No emergency service and no support hours. It only offers preparedness checklists. No reviewer describes an emergency.
The caregiver signs up with email, Apple or Google and is walked through it in a few minutes, then invites others. Works on iPhone, Android and the web. Reviewers call it simple and easy (7).

29 caregiving app reviews (23 Apple, 6 Google). No Reddit post describes using it. Possibly prompted 5-star reviews in 2025-26. Pages saved 2026-11-02. Data: docs/sources/competitive-analysis-2/themes/caring-village.json and facts/caring-village.json
CaringBridge
Direct (coordination)
Family care-coordination apps
https://www.caringbridge.org/
A private web page or app journal for health updates, with comments, a help calendar for meals and rides, and links to GoFundMe and Meal Train.
Claims to be the established nonprofit (since 1997) built only for health journeys: private, ad-free, and never selling personal data.

One update reaches everyone, so far fewer calls and texts (49 of 95). It frees the caregiver to be with the sick person (19), is easy to post and read (16), lets far-away family follow along (15), and the same page works again for each new crisis (8).

The app is the weak spot. Posting freezes or loses posts and photos (7), the app is weaker than the website (6), and the mid-2024 update broke features (4) and locked family out of sign-in (3). It isn't built for day-to-day care coordination (3), and donation requests feel pushy (2).

Strongly positive about one job, telling everyone at once. Most of the 95 caregiving items are short 5-star Google reviews from 2020 to 2023. Usually a spouse or parent posts and relatives read (14). Complaints cluster around the 2024 app redesign. On Reddit it is rarely named (7 posts).

It's a one-way news feed, so it doesn't split tasks or get siblings to help day to day (217 and 187 posts). It doesn't touch accounts, POA or records (132, 97, 67). Medications and safety (77, 59) aren't covered. Families run group texts and spreadsheets next to it for the daily work (3).
Update everyone at once about a loved one's health and gather support, so no one goes through it alone.
A free, donation-funded nonprofit: about $10.6M revenue in FY2025, 97% from contributions. It asks users for gifts, and its privacy policy also lists sharing data for targeted ads.
A patient or family caregiver creates the page, and friends and family read it. It's free for everyone. Donors fund it, often the same families (6).
No contract. People come back for comments, update alerts and journaling. Reviewers stay because it saves time in every crisis (8) and drop only the app, not the service, when posting fails (2).
A help center, video tutorials, customer care staff and online chat with a virtual or live agent. No reviewer mentions support.

Yes. The author adds co-authors, and readers use their own accounts. Private pages limit readers to an approved list. Reviewers say people follow a shared link, often without signing up (4), and more than one relative can post (2). Older relatives got locked out when sign-in changed in 2024 (2).

The creator picks public, semi-private or private, and the default lets any signed-in user see posts. It says it doesn't sell health data but shares some data for targeted ads. Page deletion is by email and can take up to 90 days. Families trust it as a private space (6).
Not stated on its pages. It isn't an emergency tool. When the app fails, families switch to the website (5).
A patient or caregiver makes a page on the web or app and sets privacy (18 and over). Reviewers say it's easy to start and restart (6), but app posting is buggy (5).

95 caregiving items: 91 app reviews (79 Google, 12 Apple) and 4 Reddit posts. 15 copied reviews removed. Mostly short and positive. Eight company pages saved as empty. Data: docs/sources/competitive-analysis-2/themes/caringbridge.json and facts/caringbridge.json

A free central place to organize meals, rides and other help from friends and family for someone in need.
Free. The saved pages don't say how it makes money. Old links hint at sponsors and partners (for example CancerCare's 'My Cancer Circle'). No funding found.
Caregivers, friends, neighbors and new parents use it. Free, and no payer is named.
No tiers or contracts. The shared task calendar and emailed announcements keep a group active. No reviewer evidence.
A small help base for members and admins, plus contact emails. No reviewer evidence.
Yes. The organizer invites people with their own logins. Admins assign roles and private groups. No reviewer evidence.
Admins can limit posts to chosen groups. Data handling and deletion aren't stated (the privacy page saved as a 404).
Not stated. Not an emergency tool.

Medisafe
Indirect (covers part of the need)
Medication reminder apps
https://medisafeapp.com/
Medication reminders and refill alerts, drug-interaction warnings, one account for several family members' meds, and a 'Medfriend' who is alerted to missed doses.
Claims to be the number-one medication reminder, ranked first by pharmacists, with complicated dosing and security certifications.
Keeps a loved one's complicated medication schedule on track (10 of 21), handles meds for several family members in one app (5), and lets a relative see from afar that doses were taken (4).

It's built for one person managing one set of meds. It's hard for more than one caregiver to share the work (4), the caregiver's view goes out of sync or loses meds (3), you can't tell whose dose or refill it is (2), alerts are unreliable (2), and setup is hard (2).

Mixed: it works for one caregiver tracking a loved one (10), and breaks when caregivers share it (4) or their views go out of sync (3). Writers are adult children (7), spouses (5) and parents of a child (3). Many reviews that passed the first filter were patients tracking their own meds (9 dropped). Reddit barely names it (1 post, an ad for a rival).

Medications only. It doesn't spread the wider care work across siblings (187 posts), and gives no help with accounts, papers, records or safety (132, 97, 67, 59). Even the medication part breaks when two caregivers share it, which Reddit also shows: medication changes not shared, near double doses (24 posts).
Never miss or double a dose, so you think less about medications and live more.

Free app with a paid subscription (price not shown, the pricing pages saved as 404s). It also sells a platform to drug makers and providers and may share de-identified data commercially. Raised a $30M Series C in 2021.

Patients and family members use it. Some users pay the subscription, and drug companies and providers are business customers. Price isn't stated. A rival's ad says it limited free users in 2026 (not confirmed).
Daily reminders, missed-dose alerts and a community, plus limited access without a subscription in some countries. Reviewers leave when the caregiver side fails (2), and fans recommend it (2).
A help center, email, a US phone number and a Facebook beta group. No reviewer theme on support.
Yes, as a 'Medfriend' (gets alerts) or 'Caregiver' (can edit). Reviewers say watching doses works (4), but sharing breaks down between linked caregivers (4).

Collects meds, prescriptions, insurance and pharmacy data. It may share with drug makers and researchers, says it isn't bound by medical secrecy, and keeps data up to 7 years. Users can delete the account in the app. No reviewer theme.
No emergency service. It warns that phone battery savers can silently stop reminders. Reviewers report unreliable alerts (2).
Download it (iPhone, Android or web) and add meds. An account is optional. Reviewers find setup hard (2).
21 caregiving app reviews (15 Apple, 6 Google). No real Reddit use. Pricing pages missing. Data: docs/sources/competitive-analysis-2/themes/medisafe.json and facts/medisafe.json
Everplans
Direct (access to accounts)
Digital vaults and emergency access
https://www.everplans.com/
A secure online vault for documents, IDs, accounts and wishes, with guided checklists and 'deputies' who get access to chosen sections.
Claims to organize all of a person's life details and tell them what to do next, using a smart planning system.
Not enough caregiver evidence to answer. Only 1 caregiving review: a child said a late father's notes made settling his estate easier.
Not enough caregiver evidence to answer. Non-caregiver reviews (people planning their own affairs) mostly say the iPad app is only a phone-size version (5 of 7).
No caregiver voice: 1 of 8 reviews comes from someone acting for another person, and none on Reddit. It's used to plan your own affairs, or after a death, not during ongoing care.

It depends on the parent organizing everything ahead of time. Reddit shows the opposite: passwords lost, codes going to the parent's phone, banks rejecting POAs (132 and 97 posts). Nothing for daily coordination, medications or safety.
Keep every important document and decision of your life in one safe place you can share with the people who will need it.
Freemium: free (3 items) or Premium at $99.99 a year, plus deals through financial advisors and partners. Owned by Precoa since October 2024.
People organizing their own affairs pay for Premium themselves, or get it through an advisor (who pays then isn't stated). $99.99 a year.
The free tier stops at 3 items, and date reminders bring people back. Cancellation terms aren't stated.
Self-serve: FAQs, a contact form, articles and checklists. No reviewer evidence on support.
Yes. The owner names deputies for chosen sections, sections can open only after death, and household co-administrators get full edit rights. No caregiver evidence.
Sensitive data is encrypted and stored with a HIPAA-compliant host, shared only with chosen deputies. The owner deletes the account themselves, but some personal data may be kept.
No emergency service. Chosen sections are released after death. It disclaims liability for lost or breached data.
The person fills in their own plan on the web or the app. Time isn't stated.
8 Apple reviews (1 caregiving), no Reddit or forum use. Too thin to judge from reviews. Data: docs/sources/competitive-analysis-2/themes/everplans.json and facts/everplans.json
Epic MyChart
Direct (access to records)
Patient portals with proxy access
https://www.mychart.org/
A patient portal: test results, doctor notes, messages to the doctor, appointments, medications, bills, and 'proxy access' to a family member's chart.
Claims scale (over 190 million patients) and one login that pulls care together across several healthcare organizations.

Once a caregiver gets in, it works. They see a loved one's results and notes (13 of 78), keep several family members under one login (12), message the doctor directly (11), track appointments and meds (11), and follow a hospital stay day by day (5).

Getting in is the problem. Older parents can't or won't use it (11), caregivers have no login of their own so families share the parent's password (7), proxy access is hard to set up (6), the parent's privacy wishes clash with family access (6), and a spouse's login keeps failing (5).

Mostly positive once access is set up, with frustration about getting it. The 78 caregiving items come mainly from adult children (42) and spouses (15). 9 are parents of minors, counted separately. It's the competitor caregivers name most on Reddit (36 posts kept).

It covers one clinic system's records. It doesn't solve banks, insurers or other accounts (132 posts), shares nothing with siblings except by screenshots (3), and doesn't coordinate tasks, safety or caregiver support. Each clinic sets proxy rules, so access is uneven.
See and manage all your medical information and care in one place.
Not stated on its page. It is licensed by Epic to healthcare organizations, and patients reach it through their provider. Epic's revenue was about $5.7B in FY2024.
Patients and their family use it. Healthcare organizations license it. Free to patients, as far as reviews show (no item mentions a price). Caregivers pay the parent's medical bills through it (5).
Not stated. Patients don't choose it, their clinic does. Caregivers stay because it becomes essential (4) but feel let down when it matters most (3).

Split: care questions go to the clinic, technical questions go to Epic by email. Reviewers say messages and refill requests go unanswered (3), and there is little help when a loved one's account is locked (2).

Through 'proxy access' set up by each healthcare organization. Some families get it working (6), but many find it hard (8) or share the parent's password instead (7). Siblings get updates by screenshot (3).

The saved page only covers two-step login and scam warnings, and deletion goes through the clinic. Reviewers say the parent's privacy wishes clash with family access (6) and security steps get in caregivers' way (3).
Not for emergencies: it tells people to call 911. In urgent moments app messages didn't replace a phone call (4).
The patient creates an account with their clinic's MyChart. Getting caregiver access set up is the hard part (6). Easy day to day once set up (5).

78 caregiving items: 42 Google and Apple reviews and 36 Reddit posts. The Apple reviews cover only one week. Only the home page was saved, so company answers are thin. Data: docs/sources/competitive-analysis-2/themes/mychart.json and facts/mychart.json
Lively
Direct (monitoring and safety)
Remote monitoring and medical alert
https://www.lively.com/
Jitterbug senior phones and a medical alert device with a 24/7 urgent-response button, optional fall detection, nurses on call, and the Lively Link app that lets family see alerts and location.
Claims its people set it apart: 100% US-based agents, nurses on call and ride booking, on easy senior phones with no long-term contract.

When it works, it reassures the family (25 of 193). They can see where the person is (23), the button reaches a quick, helpful operator (15), low-battery alerts let family remind the person to charge (11), and the phone is simple enough for the older person (7).

The family app is unreliable. Location is wrong or stale (58), support is slow or can't fix it (40), sign-in fails or the app crashes (37), the device shows as off when it's on (28), and alerts to family come late or never (27). Linking family is confusing (13), and people pay for a service that doesn't work with no refund (11).

Mostly negative about the family app, positive about the operators. Buyers are adult children far away (12) and spouses (9), often for dementia (8). 14 say they're leaving because it's unreliable. Most reviews are from 2015 to 2020, with location and notification bugs again in 2024-26.

It watches one person's safety. The family side, being told reliably and fast, is where it fails (27). Families want alerts to reach them, not only a dispatcher (Reddit, 59 safety posts). Nothing for sharing tasks, accounts, papers or records (187, 132, 97, 67).
Older adults stay independent and protected with easy phones and one-button help, while family feels reassured.
Device plus monthly service plans and add-ons, plus a $99 a year caregiver bundle of partner services. Part of Best Buy Health (Best Buy bought it for $800M in 2018).

The older adult wears or carries it. Adult children or spouses usually buy it and hold the account (5). Alert device $89.99, plans $24.99 or $34.99 a month, fall detection +$9.99 a month. Reviewers split: good value (6) versus paying for something that fails (11).
Monthly plans with no long-term contract, plus an auto-renewing caregiver bundle. Reviewers who stay do so for one key reason despite problems (6). 14 are leaving, and cancelling is hard (3).

Phone-first human support: US agents 24/7, Nurse On-Call, care advocates, stores. Reviewers split: friendly support (7) versus slow or unable to fix the problem (40), with replies taking days or weeks (10).

Yes. The owner invites family to Lively Link, and they get alerts and location. Several relatives often follow one person (10), but linking is confusing (13), and following two people in one app is hard (2).
Barely stated: family see location when an alert fires, and the privacy policy wasn't saved. Reviewers raise privacy worries (4), and more often lose trust in it with a loved one's safety (10).

The button reaches US agents 24/7 who send help or call a caregiver. Fall detection is a paid add-on. Reviewers: quick, helpful operator (15), but emergencies handled badly or family not told (10), and missed falls (4).

Buy online or in a store, activate and pick a plan, then family install the app on their phones. Reviewers say it's hard for the older person (13), linking is confusing (13), and fixes need reboots the older person can't do (9).

193 caregiving items, mostly reviews of the Lively Link family app (177 reviews: 112 Apple, 65 Google), plus 15 Reddit posts and 1 forum thread describing real use. Many complaints repeat the same app versions. Data: docs/sources/competitive-analysis-2/themes/lively.json and facts/lively.json
Medical Guardian
Direct (monitoring and safety)
Remote monitoring and medical alert
https://www.medicalguardian.com/
Medical alert devices for home and on the go, with a 24/7 monitoring center, GPS, optional fall detection, and the MyMedicalGuardian family app.
Claims to be faster and more personal than calling 911 because the center already knows who and where you are. Also its lightest device, with 5-day battery, and an AARP 'Best Overall' award.
Help comes fast when the button is pressed (5 of 52), families get peace of mind and the parent more independence (5), and checking on a parent from your phone is the main reason to buy (7).

The family app fails. It won't sign in or errors (16), steps, battery and location are wrong (9), support gives different answers or long waits (7), fall detection misses falls or false-alarms (7), and family isn't told when something happens (6). Parents stop wearing it (5), and there are extra fees and hard refunds (5).

Mostly negative about the family app (39 of 52 items are app reviews, mostly 1-star, 2024-25 after a forced update). Positive about the button itself. Buyers are adult children watching from afar (10). 8 cancel, return or plan to leave.

Family appear only as emergency contacts. There's no real family login on its pages, and the app that exists is unreliable. Families can't trust the data shown (9). Nothing for sharing care work, accounts, papers or records (187, 132, 97, 67).
One button gets you to a 24/7 monitoring center that sends the right help fast, at home or on the go.
Devices with ongoing (often yearly) monitoring subscriptions, with the device often free with a promo. Also sold through dealers, health plans and senior living. No funding figure found.

The older adult wears it, and adult children usually arrange it (10). About $1 a day. Some insurance may cover it. Reviewers report $400 a year, $80 a month for two devices, and $120 a year extra for fall detection (3).
Ongoing subscriptions with possible cancellation fees. Reviewers cancel, return or plan to leave (8), and parents stop wearing it (5).
A 24/7 US monitoring center, a member support line and sales consultants. Reviewers say support gives different answers, long waits or rudeness (7).
Not described on its pages: family are emergency contacts only. Reviewers say several relatives get called after an alert (2), but app access is uneven or gets lost (2).
Only marketing consent is stated (AI chat, recorded calls, texts). The privacy policy wasn't saved. Reviewers mostly say they can't trust the data shown (9). No reviewer raises privacy.

The button reaches a 24/7 US center that sends EMS or a contact. The company warns fall detection doesn't always work. Reviewers: fast help (5), but the response failed or was slow in a real emergency (4).
Order by phone or online, free activation, worn on the neck or wrist. Reviewers say the family app won't sign in (16) and setup fails to connect or save (5).
